mainEntity.name: What causes micro-gaps to form in dental crowns?

acceptedAnswer.text: Micro-gaps at crown margins can arise from several factors. Inaccuracies in the physical impression of the tooth, variations during laboratory fabrication, cement dissolution over time, and changes to the underlying tooth structure can all contribute. In some cases, minor discrepancies in fit are present from the time of placement. Digital scanning and CAD/CAM milling aim to reduce the dimensional variability in the fabrication process, though the clinical outcome also depends on tooth preparation technique, material choice, and ongoing oral care.

mainEntity.name: Are custom-milled crowns better than traditional crowns?

acceptedAnswer.text: Custom-milled crowns offer certain advantages in terms of the precision of digital fabrication and consistency of dimensional accuracy. However, "better" depends entirely on the individual clinical situation. Traditional laboratory-fabricated crowns, produced by skilled technicians, can also achieve excellent results. Your dentist will consider the specific needs of your tooth, your bite, aesthetic requirements, and other factors to recommend the most appropriate type of crown for you. A clinical assessment is necessary before any treatment recommendation can be made.

mainEntity.name: How long do custom-milled crowns typically last?

acceptedAnswer.text: The longevity of any dental crown depends on multiple factors, including the material used, the clinical condition of the underlying tooth, the patient's bite and habits (such as teeth grinding), and the quality of daily oral hygiene. Custom-milled ceramic crowns can be durable restorations, but no specific lifespan can be guaranteed. Regular dental examinations allow your dentist to monitor the condition of your crown and identify any early signs of wear, damage, or marginal deterioration that may require attention.

mainEntity.name: Can I feel a micro-gap in my crown?

acceptedAnswer.text: Micro-gaps are generally very small and are not typically detectable by feel alone. However, if a gap is present and has allowed bacteria to penetrate, you may notice symptoms such as sensitivity to cold, sweetness, or pressure around the crowned tooth, or occasional mild discomfort at the gumline. Some patients with marginal issues remain asymptomatic for a period. This is why regular dental check-ups — including radiographic examination of crowned teeth — are important for detecting problems that may not yet be causing noticeable symptoms.

mainEntity.name: Is same-day crown treatment with CAD/CAM technology reliable?

acceptedAnswer.text: Chairside CAD/CAM systems that mill crowns within a single appointment have become increasingly common and are used successfully in many dental practices. They offer the convenience of completing treatment in one visit and eliminate the need for a temporary crown. The reliability of same-day milled crowns depends on the quality of the digital scan, the milling equipment used, the material selected, and the clinical expertise of the treating dentist. As with all dental treatment, an individual consultation is required to assess whether this approach is suitable for a specific tooth and clinical situation.

mainEntity.name: Do I need a crown if my tooth is only slightly damaged?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not every damaged or weakened tooth requires a crown. Depending on the extent of the damage, your dentist may recommend alternative restorations such as an inlay, onlay, or composite filling. A crown is typically considered when a tooth has significant structural loss, has undergone root canal treatment, or requires protection from further fracture. The appropriate restoration can only be determined following a thorough clinical examination, which may include dental X-rays to assess the extent of any underlying damage or decay.
